chunks: "Redundancy means having more than one way to do a critical function, so a single failure doesn't take the whole system down.

You use it when the cost of failure is high, like safety-critical systems in cars, aircraft and medical devices, or when you can't get to the system to fix it, like a satellite, or when downtime is very expensive, like a server farm.
There are a few ways to build it. Active or parallel redundancy runs two or more units all the time. Standby redundancy keeps a spare ready and switches over when the main fails.
For logic or sensors you can run three and vote, called triple modular redundancy, which masks one bad channel.
At the circuit level an easy example is two power inputs combined with diodes or ideal-diode controllers, so either one can power the load. The catches are important.

You need a way to detect the failure, the switch or voter becomes a new single point of failure, and redundancy doesn't help if all copies fail for the same reason, like a shared power rail or identical software bug.
So you'd add independence, such as different suppliers or even different designs, and you'd pay in cost, weight, power and complexity.
If it isn't safety-critical or hard to reach, simpler and cheaper is usually the better engineering."
